name: post-trade-cooldown-30m
rationale: Literature-motivated. Today's baseline at the 500,000 JPY diagnostic capital makes 765 trades in 14 days (54.6/day) split 380 buys / 385 sells -- a 0.987 ratio -- at a win_rate of 0.108, i.e. nine trades in ten lose. That is the signature of a position oscillating across one threshold rather than of directional trading, and it is the fourth consecutive run to show it. shirube has no notion of a minimum holding period at all: the moment an order fills, the very next 1-minute candle may produce an opposite-signed delta that clears allocation_threshold and reverses it, paying the spread twice for a round trip that lasted 60 seconds. Kearns, Kulesza & Nevmyvaka (arXiv:1007.2593, key claim below) bound the profitability of exactly this regime -- market orders only, holding periods of seconds to minutes -- and find it 'surprisingly modest' even for a trader with perfect foresight, because execution cost is paid per round trip while edge accrues with holding time. This hypothesis adds the one control shirube lacks: after a fill, no new order for a fixed cooldown. It is deliberately distinct from the two adjacent rejected variants -- rebalance-spacing-15m paced *evaluation* on a fixed clock whether or not anything traded (and at 50,000 JPY that let the delta accumulate and RAISED turnover 58%), and reversal-hysteresis-multiplier raised the bar only for opposite-signed deltas but never blocked anything in time. A cooldown is triggered by a fill, keyed on the candle clock, and blocks continuations and reversals alike.
code_change_summary: Add a post-fill cooldown that suppresses new orders for a fixed interval after any order that actually filled. Introduce a named private constant with a doc comment stating the value, the unit and its source: POST_TRADE_COOLDOWN_SECS = 1800 (30 minutes), chosen as 30x the 60s bar so it spans the shortest indicator period in experiments/baseline-config.json's neighbourhood without approaching the 200-bar SMA; state in the comment that the value is a round figure picked a priori and NOT fitted on any window, holdout or training. Implement it in BOTH places so live and backtest cannot diverge -- the 2026-09-09 report records a filter that is live in one and dead in the other as a trap that makes every future backtest number untransferable: (a) src/backtest/simulator.rs, in Simulator::run's per-candle loop -- track `last_fill_time: Option<DateTime<Utc>>` and, before the `delta.abs() >= trading_config.allocation_threshold` check around line 157, skip the whole order path when `candle.open_time - last_fill < POST_TRADE_COOLDOWN_SECS`; set last_fill_time to `candle.open_time` only on the RiskDecision::Allow branch where `exchange.send_order` is actually called, never on a delta that was gated, dropped under the lot size, or rejected by the risk manager. (b) src/trading/engine.rs, as a `last_fill_at: Option<DateTime<Utc>>` field on TradingEngine, checked in both order paths (the `delta.abs() < allocation_threshold` sites in handle_indicator and handle_rebalance) and set in submit_order only on the branch where send_order returned Ok. Use the candle/indicator timestamp in the backtest and Utc::now() live, mirroring how RiskManager::observe_time already takes the candle clock in the simulator (see its NOTE on why wall-clock would be wrong there). The cooldown must only ever SUPPRESS an order the current logic would have placed; it must never enable one, change an order's side or size, or alter the sticky target -- sticky_target must keep updating during a cooldown so that the target the engine resumes from is current, not stale. Add unit tests covering: an order placed at t, an opposite-signed delta at t+60s being suppressed, the same delta at t+1801s being allowed, and that a suppressed candle does not update last_fill_time (so the cooldown cannot extend itself indefinitely). Report in step 3 how many orders the cooldown suppressed at each capital, not just the report JSON -- the mechanism's behaviour is what distinguishes a real effect from a lot-floor artifact.
constraints: MUST NOT modify the body or the signature of TradingEngine::compute_btc_target. This hypothesis gates WHEN an order may be placed, after the allocation target has already been computed; the allocation formula itself is out of scope.
This change MUST be made only on this hypothesis's own dedicated isolation: "worktree" branch -- never as a direct commit to dev/main.
MUST apply the cooldown at both the live sites in src/trading/engine.rs and the backtest site in src/backtest/simulator.rs, so live and backtest behaviour cannot diverge.

MUST pass `cargo test`, including the existing compute_btc_target_* and Simulator unit tests -- update expected values only where the cooldown legitimately changes them, and do not weaken or delete a test just to make it pass.

MUST NOT fit POST_TRADE_COOLDOWN_SECS on the holdout window, or on any window at all. It is an a priori round number; if it turns out to be wrong, that is a result to report, not a value to retune mid-run.

MUST NOT depend on PR #21 (enabling/backtest-rebalance-interval) or on TradingConfig::rebalance_interval_secs in any way -- that field's live-versus-backtest semantics are an open human question and this hypothesis must be scoreable without resolving it.

A promoted change still becomes its own PR against dev (per the pipeline's step 6) and is never merged automatically -- a human reviews it like any other algorithm hypothesis. Flag explicitly in the PR description that this diff changes when live orders are placed, since it adds a gate on the live order path.

MUST NOT touch src/exchange/bitflyer/*, .github/workflows/*, or the order-submission mechanics themselves (the cooldown decides whether allocation_delta_to_order is called; it must not change how an order is built or sent).

paper_reference.title: Empirical Limitations on High Frequency Trading Profitability
paper_reference.authors: Michael Kearns, Alex Kulesza, Yuriy Nevmyvaka
paper_reference.key_claim: Simulating an idealized trader with PERFECT FORESIGHT but restricted to market orders and short holding periods, the authors estimate the maximum possible profitability of aggressive high-frequency practices and 'arrive at figures that are surprisingly modest' -- their stated subject is 'the tension between execution costs and trading horizon confronted by high-frequency traders', i.e. execution cost is paid per round trip while realizable edge grows with holding time, so shrinking the holding period caps profit from above regardless of signal quality.
paper_reference.pros: It is an upper bound rather than a strategy claim, which is exactly the right kind of evidence for shirube's situation: the pipeline's standing finding (docs/self-improvement-loop.md, 'Benchmarks') is that the strategy has no measured gross alpha and loses to its own exposure held statically, and this paper says that a market-order strategy with minute-scale holding periods has a low profit ceiling even with a perfect signal. shirube matches the paper's restricted setting on both axes it identifies -- market orders only (MockExchangeClient fills a buy at the ask and a sell at the bid, so a round trip pays ~2x slippage_pct by construction) and holding periods of one to a few 60s bars. The prescribed remedy, lengthening the holding period, is expressible without a new indicator, a new config field, or any change to the signal.
paper_reference.cons: 2010 US equities on a Nasdaq order book, roughly fifteen years and one asset class away from BTC/JPY spot on bitFlyer, with entirely different tick size, fee structure, and no 24/7 session -- the quantitative bound does not transfer and no number from it is used here. It is a perfect-foresight ceiling, so it constrains what is achievable but says nothing about whether any particular cooldown length improves a real strategy; a cooldown could equally well suppress the few trades that were working. It predates BTC's current liquidity and derivatives regime entirely. And the specific value of 30 minutes is not the paper's -- the paper offers no cooldown parameter at all, so the mechanism is motivated by it while the parameter is arbitrary. shirube's own backtest gate decides, exactly as docs/self-improvement-loop.md requires.
